lead: A gesture interface reads the shape and motion of your hand and turns it into a command, so no button or stick is needed. It exists because the hand is already a precise, many-jointed tool: you point at a menu, curl your fingers to grab, flick to scroll. A data glove is the direct way to measure hand shape — bend sensors along each finger report how far it is curled. Gesture interfaces appear in VR menus, AR assembly guidance, sign-language capture, and teleoperation of robots.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for what makes an input device good, Chapter 2.2 for 6-DOF tracking of the hand, and Chapter 2.3 for selection, which a gesture often replaces.

blocks.text: A gesture interface is an input device plus software that turns the shape or motion of a hand into a command, with no button or stick in between. Reading the hand directly is attractive because the hand carries more than twenty degrees of freedom. Gestures often replace the selection step of Chapter 2.3; using gestures for system control is covered in Unit 5.

items: Static posture: the hand shape alone, held still, carries the meaning — a flat palm, a pinch.
Dynamic gesture: the meaning is in the movement over time — a swipe, a wave, a circle drawn in air.
Contact versus non-contact: in a contact interface hardware touches the hand (a glove, a ring); in a non-contact one a camera, depth sensor or radar watches from a distance.

Symbolic, deictic, manipulative: a symbolic gesture is a learned sign such as thumbs-up for OK; a deictic gesture points at a target, meaning "that one"; a manipulative gesture grabs, moves or turns an object.
Flex-sensor glove: a thin resistive strip runs along each finger. Bending stretches the strip and its resistance rises, so a voltage divider gives a bend reading.
Fibre-optic glove: light runs through a looped fibre and bending lets some escape, so the light reaching the detector falls as the finger curls. No electrical parts sit on the finger.
Resistive-ink glove: bend-sensitive ink is printed on fabric. Cheap, but the reading drifts as the fabric stretches.
Pinch glove: contact sensors between the thumb and each fingertip. It reports touch, not how hard you press.
6-DOF wand with buttons: a tracked handle from Chapter 2.2. The command is button plus motion; hand shape is ignored entirely.
Bare-hand camera tracking: nothing is worn, but fingers hide each other, which the skeleton fitting of Chapter 2.5 must resolve.
EMG armband: electrodes on the forearm read muscle activity and can catch intent a few tens of milliseconds before the finger moves. Noisy, and trained per user.

blocks.text: Contact devices give a reliable hand shape and work when the hand is out of camera view. Non-contact devices keep the hand free but lose accuracy when fingers overlap.

sections.h3: From sensor readings to a gesture event

items: Sense: each sensor outputs a voltage that falls or rises with bend.
Amplify and digitise: an ADC turns the voltage into counts, for example 8 bits giving 256 counts over the full bend range.
Calibrate: record the open-hand and fist reading of every sensor for this user and map each to 0–1.
Segment: find where the gesture starts and ends, using a rest threshold, a velocity trigger, or a fixed window of frames.
Extract features: normalised bend per sensor, fingertip distances, and speed.

Classify: template matching takes the smallest Euclidean distance to stored feature vectors; dynamic time warping (DTW) matches a template to the same gesture made at a different speed; a hidden Markov model (HMM) suits a gesture built from ordered stages; a small neural net classifies a window of raw frames.
Decide: apply hysteresis to the score (enter high, leave low) and a confidence threshold, then wait a few frames of debounce.

blocks.text: accept g* if p(g* | x) ≥ τ
blocks.where: g* is the most likely gesture class, x is the feature window, p is the classifier's score, and τ is the confidence threshold (often 0.8); below τ the event is rejected as no gesture.

items: Sensor count: 10 sensors is common, roughly two per finger. The hand has about 27 bones in many coupled joints, so 10 readings are not 10 independent joint angles.
Resolution: bend range ÷ 2^(ADC bits). A 180° range on 8 bits gives 180 ÷ 256 ≈ 0.70° per count.
Sample rate: 100 Hz is standard, because hand motion has little energy above about 20 Hz.
Repeatability: the same pose read twice should agree to within a few degrees.
Calibration is per user and per sensor: a glove calibrated on one hand misreads another.
Comfort over a session: heat and sweat under the fabric, cable drag, a minute or two to put on, and sensor zero drifting as the glove warms or shifts on the hand.

figure.caption: Bend readings travel from the glove sensors to a single gesture event. Notice that per-user calibration sits between digitising and classification, that segmentation and feature extraction come before classification, and that the last step is a threshold with hysteresis, not one raw reading.

examples.question: A data glove has 10 flex sensors, each read by an 8-bit ADC over a bend range of 0° to 180°, and it samples at 100 Hz. (a) What is the bend resolution in degrees per count? (b) How many bytes per second does the raw stream carry, counting one byte per sensor? (c) How many samples fall inside a 2-second calibration pose? (d) The fist threshold is 140° and the sensor jitters by ±3°. What goes wrong, and what two thresholds fix it?
steps: (a) An 8-bit ADC gives 2⁸ = 256 counts across the whole range.
(a) Resolution = 180° ÷ 256 = 0.703125°, that is about 0.70° per count.
(b) One frame carries one byte per sensor = 10 bytes. At 100 frames per second the stream is 10 × 100 = 1000 bytes per second.
(c) Samples in the pose = 100 Hz × 2 s = 200 samples.
(d) A 140° bend with ±3° jitter reads anywhere from 137° to 143°, so the reading crosses 140° on almost every sample: the fist fires, releases and fires again.

(d) The hysteresis band must be wider than the ±3° jitter band, otherwise a finger held near 140° still reaches both thresholds. Take a 5° margin: enter at 140 + 5 = 145° and leave at 140 − 5 = 135°. Between 135° and 145° the state holds, so one fist gives one event.
examples.answer: Resolution 0.70° per count, stream 1000 bytes per second, 200 samples in the pose, and the fix is enter at 145°, leave at 135° — a band wider than the ±3° jitter.
examples.check:
bend_max = 180
bits = 8
sensors = 10
rate = 100
pose_s = 2
thr = 140
jitter = 3
margin = 5
res = bend_max / (2 ** bits)
bytes_per_s = sensors * rate
samples = rate * pose_s
enter = thr + margin
leave = thr - margin
print(res)
print(bytes_per_s)
print(samples)
print(enter)
print(leave)

traps: Counting flex sensors as degrees of freedom: a 10-sensor glove does not give 10 independent joint angles, because finger joints are coupled and move together.
One threshold without hysteresis: a held gesture then repeats every frame instead of firing once.
Mixing static posture with dynamic gesture: a pose needs one frame, a swipe needs a window of frames and a segmenter.
Mixing deictic with symbolic: pointing at a target is deictic; a thumbs-up meaning OK is symbolic whatever it points at.
Forgetting calibration: a glove calibrated on one user reads another user's fist as a half-curl.

quiz.a: An input device plus software that converts hand or body posture and motion into commands, with no mechanical control such as a button or stick in between.

quiz.q: Why does a fibre-optic bend sensor need no electrical parts on the finger?
quiz.a: The bend changes how much light escapes from the fibre; only the light source and detector sit away from the finger, so the finger carries a passive glass loop.

quiz.q: A glove has 12 sensors read by a 10-bit ADC over 0° to 180°, sampling at 120 Hz. Find the bend resolution and the raw stream rate with one byte per sensor.
quiz.a: Counts = 2¹⁰ = 1024. Resolution = 180 ÷ 1024 ≈ 0.176° per count. Stream = 12 × 120 = 1440 bytes per second.

quiz.q: A user reports that one grab produces two grab events. Give two probable causes and the cure.
quiz.a: The threshold sits inside the sensor jitter band, or the segmenter re-triggers on the same hold. Cure: hysteresis (enter high, leave low) plus a debounce time of a few frames.

quiz.q: Why does bare-hand camera tracking lose accuracy where a glove does not?
quiz.a: Fingers hide each other from the camera and lighting changes the image, so the shape must be guessed; a glove measures each finger directly and cannot be occluded.

quiz.q: An 8-sensor glove samples at 100 Hz with one byte per sensor. How many bytes does a 1.5-second gesture carry?
quiz.a: Bytes per second = 8 × 100 = 800. Over 1.5 s: 800 × 1.5 = 1200 bytes.

quiz.q: Why must a dynamic gesture be classified with DTW or an HMM rather than plain template matching?
quiz.a: The same gesture made faster or slower stretches in time, so fixed-length Euclidean matching fails; DTW aligns the time axis and an HMM models the ordered stages of the movement.

beyond: Not for the exam. Commercial hand tracking has moved to camera-based systems built into headsets, while stretch sensors and IMU rings compete with gloves on comfort. Surface EMG on the forearm is used in research and in wristbands that infer a pinch or a tap with no finger hardware at all. Fibre-optic and printed-ink gloves remain common in motion capture and in teleoperation of surgical robots. Useful search terms: stretch-sensor hand tracking, surface EMG gesture recognition, dataglove calibration.
